section_summary: This section centers on suspected Japanese intelligence-gathering in Hawaii, including detailed military and legal assessments of visits by Japanese naval tankers, photography and surveying near strategic facilities, local contacts, and the applicability of federal and territorial laws. It also contains correspondence about alleged Japanese propaganda in California schools, State Department handling of Korean activist Kilsoo Haan, and proposals for Korean independence advocacy. The final page introduces material criticizing Japanese-language schools and an anonymous appeal opposing Hawaiian statehood because of the islands’ Japanese population.

subfiles.title: Letter concerning Japan Where Ancient Loyalties Survive
subfiles.from: V. S. McClatchy, California Joint Immigration Committee
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Department of State
subfiles.about: McClatchy defends his committee’s campaign against an Institute of Pacific Relations schoolbook that it considered misleading and pro-Japanese.
subfiles.summary: McClatchy says California's Board of Education lacked jurisdiction to ban 'Japan Where Ancient Loyalties Survive', so the committee will approach school districts; he links it to a Japanese cultural-propaganda program and says the revision hid distortions by omission.

subfiles.title: Note on Moore’s conversation with General Embick
subfiles.about: Hackworth records that Moore told General Embick the State Department was available to discuss the matter with the War Department.
subfiles.summary: Note: Moore offered General Embick State Department cooperation whenever War wishes to discuss the subject.

subfiles.title: Handwritten routing note to Mr. Moore
subfiles.from: Office of the Legal Adviser, author illegible
subfiles.about: An almost wholly illegible handwritten note appears to return or forward material to Moore for his consideration.
subfiles.summary: Short handwritten routing note to Mr. Moore; OCR insufficient for reading.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on waiver of jury trial in Hawaii
subfiles.from: Office of the Legal Adviser, Department of State
subfiles.about: The memorandum examines whether Hawaii’s statutory authorization of nonjury criminal trials is compatible with the United States Constitution.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum quotes Hawaii’s law permitting defendants in noncapital criminal cases to waive a jury, then reviews Article III, the Sixth Amendment, and authorities concerning waiver in federal and state courts. It traces congressional extension of the Constitution and federal laws to the Territory of Hawaii through the Organic Act and its amendments. Relying particularly on Hawaii v. Mankichi, it concludes that the Constitution was formally extended to Hawaii after June 14, 1900, distinguishing the earlier prosecution involved in that case.

subfiles.title: List of proposed navigation and defense legislation
subfiles.from: Office of the Legal Adviser, Department of State
subfiles.about: The sheet lists bills regulating foreign-owned vessels and fisheries and prohibiting unauthorized images or maps of military and naval installations.
subfiles.summary: List of proposed legislation: S. 1815/H.R. 5705 and S. 4495 section 3 on navigation and fisheries, and S. 92/H.R. 3436 restricting photographs of vital defense installations.

subfiles.title: Letter to Hamilton concerning the Hawaii espionage file
subfiles.about: Moore explains his limited recollection of earlier consultations and returns Hackworth’s legal file on the matter.
subfiles.summary: Moore says he did not know of any action until shown the memo; Hackworth prepared an extensive legal memorandum; he forwards Hackworth's retained file.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to Moore forwarding confidential correspondence
subfiles.about: Far Eastern Affairs alerts Moore to confidential correspondence concerning Japanese espionage in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Memo forwards strictly confidential correspondence on Japanese espionage in Hawaii, which Moore said Bland wrote him about.

subfiles.title: White House letter establishing an interdepartmental committee
subfiles.about: Roosevelt forwards the War and Navy Departments’ secret material on Hawaii and creates an interdepartmental committee to seek a practical response.
subfiles.summary: Roosevelt sends the Secretary of State the joint War-Navy letter of October 22, 1936, designating the Secretary of War to chair a committee and keeping the material secret.

subfiles.title: Joint War and Navy letter on Japanese espionage in Hawaii
subfiles.from: Harry H. Woodring, Secretary of War, and Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: The service secretaries recommend coordinated government action and renewed legislation to reduce Japanese espionage risks in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Joint War-Navy letter: complete suppression of espionage is impracticable without drastic Hawaiian restrictions; cites executive orders and failed bills on alien fishing vessels and photography; urges cooperation under several statutes.

subfiles.title: Opinion of the Judge Advocate General on Japanese activities in Hawaii
subfiles.from: Judge Advocate General of the Navy
subfiles.about: The opinion determines whether reported intelligence-gathering by Japanese naval and civilian personnel in Hawaii could be prosecuted under existing federal and territorial law.
subfiles.summary: The opinion concludes that the federal Espionage Act applies fully in Hawaii and may cover photography from the Royal Hawaiian Hotel, surveying near Kamuela, and measurements and photographs made during the tanker Ondo’s visit to Hilo. It also surveys Hawaiian statutes on criminal syndicalism, secret associations, unauthorized military organizations, and disloyal speech, as well as the territorial and federal judicial machinery available for enforcement. A lengthy discussion of the 1911 United States-Japan Treaty of Commerce and Navigation finds that treaty rights must be respected but do not immunize espionage or violations of territorial law. The office recommends investigation, prosecution, administrative vigilance, and possible diplomatic representations, while concluding that additional statutory authority is unnecessary if officials are willing and able to act on adequate proof.

subfiles.title: Report of the Local Joint Planning Committee on Japanese government vessels
subfiles.to: Commanding General, Hawaiian Department, and Commandant, Fourteenth Naval District
subfiles.about: The committee reports intelligence concerns arising from Japanese naval tankers and training vessels visiting the Hawaiian Islands.
subfiles.summary: The report lists Japanese cruisers, oil tankers, and training vessels that visited Hawaii, noting the extra distance involved and the absence of an evident commercial reason for many calls. It describes shore tours, photography, surveying, contacts with local Japanese residents, alleged observation of American maneuvers, the Tsurumi’s passage near Midway, and nationalist propaganda directed at Hawaii’s Japanese community. It emphasizes the strategic vulnerability of the Kona coast and the proximity of Jaluit, then forwards the findings to the War and Navy Departments. Page 257 is a nearly blank trailing or separator page associated with the report packet.

subfiles.title: Report on the visit of the Japanese naval tanker Ondo
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Hawaiian Department
subfiles.about: Gilchrist reports suspicious activities and local contacts connected with Ondo’s April 1936 call at Hilo.
subfiles.summary: Report on the Japanese naval tanker Ondo: crewmen measured, sketched and photographed Hilo docks, officers toured with local Japanese hosts; Gilchrist profiles contacts like Kawasaki and concludes the Ondo sought information and criticizes lax controls.

subfiles.title: Carter letter forwarding information about Japanese officers near Waimea
subfiles.about: Carter forwards A. A. Akina’s report of Japanese officers conducting suspicious activity near Waimea after a tanker’s visit to Hilo.
subfiles.summary: Carter encloses Akina's letter on a ranch employee, notes a Japanese tanker left Hilo April 19, and offers further inquiries.

subfiles.title: Akina letter reporting surveying activity at Kamuela
subfiles.about: Akina records Mrs. Kanakanui’s account of uniformed Japanese men apparently observing and mapping the country around Kamuela.
subfiles.summary: Akina: Mrs. Kanakanui saw ten uniformed Japanese and three civilians with optical instrument and cases taking bearings in a house at Kamuela, hiding when a milk car came; Ishida and a Honolulu man took a census and distributed Mikado portraits.

subfiles.title: Anderson report on Kango Kawasaki
subfiles.to: J. Walter Doyle, Collector of Customs
subfiles.about: Anderson explains why customs officials considered Kango Kawasaki’s dealings with visiting Japanese ships suspicious.
subfiles.summary: Anderson says Kawasaki welcomed Japanese ships, assisted officers, joined photography tours and challenged customs; he has no concrete proof of government ties but sees a strong circumstantial case.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet on Hawaiian-born Japanese and nationality legislation
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to correspondence on proposed nationality-law revisions prompted by former members of Japan’s armed forces living in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: a secret Military Intelligence report on Hawaiian-born Japanese and former Japanese military personnel in Hawaii, with a War Department draft bill to restrict their entry.

subfiles.title: White House memorandum requesting a reply to Kilsoo Haan
subfiles.from: M. H. McIntyre, Secretary to the President
subfiles.about: McIntyre forwards Haan’s letter and asks the State Department to draft an appropriate reply.
subfiles.summary: White House asks State to prepare a response to Kilsoo Haan's letter.

subfiles.title: Haan request for an interview with President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Haan asks McIntyre to arrange a five-minute presidential interview so he can personally deliver a confidential Far Eastern report.
subfiles.summary: Haan wants to hand Roosevelt a confidential Far East report in late September, citing Rankin and Gillette as references.

subfiles.title: State Department recommendation not to answer Haan
subfiles.from: George T. Summerlin, Chief of Protocol
subfiles.about: Summerlin advises the White House not to acknowledge Haan’s request for a presidential interview.
subfiles.summary: Summerlin identifies Haan as a Korean (pen name W. K. Lyhan) of the Sino-Korean People's League who sent repeated letters alleging Japanese activities in Hawaii; he recommends filing without reply.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Haan’s proposed speaking tour
subfiles.about: The division reviews naval correspondence about Haan and concludes that no State Department action is warranted.
subfiles.summary: Memo: Admiral Leahy's enclosure holds a naval report and Haan's letter seeking speaking opportunities; naval authorities thought him less important than he claimed, so no action.

subfiles.title: Navy transmittal of material on Kilsoo Haan
subfiles.about: The Navy forwards a Twelfth Naval District report and enclosure concerning Haan’s planned activities in the United States.
subfiles.summary: Navy transmits the Commandant's September 8 report on Kilsoo Haan's proposed US activities, stamped received September 24, 1938.

subfiles.title: Twelfth Naval District report on Kilsoo Haan
subfiles.from: Commandant, Twelfth Naval District and Operating Base
subfiles.to: Chief of Naval Operations, Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: The report summarizes Haan’s affiliations, travel plans, and perceived lack of importance.
subfiles.summary: Twelfth Naval District: Haan, a Honolulu-based Korean and Sino-Korean People's League representative, arrives September 28 for a speaking tour on Korean freedom; considered less important than his correspondence suggests.

subfiles.title: Haan letter seeking California speaking engagements
subfiles.to: D. Kaltenbach, California Joint Immigration Committee
subfiles.about: Haan asks Kaltenbach to arrange speaking, press, and organizational contacts for his proposed Korean-independence campaign.
subfiles.summary: Haan is organizing Korean leaders to demand a plebiscite, plans a four-to-six-week US tour, and seeks California engagements on Korean freedom, Hawaiian statehood and Japanese influence.

subfiles.title: Comment on Japanese-language schools in Hawaii
subfiles.about: The excerpt summarizes a Mita Hyoron article assessing the size and character of Japanese-language education in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: About 200 Japanese-language schools in Hawaii with 40,000 pupils among 140,000 Japanese; Prof. Kiyooka found girls at Makkalei School superior to boys.

subfiles.title: Anonymous letter to President Roosevelt opposing Hawaiian statehood
subfiles.about: An anonymous correspondent urges Roosevelt to investigate what the writer describes as the Japanese peril in Hawaii and argues against territorial statehood.
subfiles.summary: Anonymous letter urges Roosevelt to send an inconspicuous investigator on Japanese influence, claims visiting senators were misled, and argues against Hawaiian statehood with racist objections; continues beyond this section.
